The decay of the $B^0_s$ meson into the $K^+K^-$ pair has a significantly lower detection rate due to the final state's narrow opening angle and associated challenges in identification. As a consequence, the current estimate of the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ lifetime obtained from the Lambert et al. measurement using $pp$ collisions at the LHC with a confidence interval of 95% is 0.496$\pm$0.048 ps. By systematically analyzing the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay sample and comparing it to other decay modes such as $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-\mu^+\mu^-$ and $B^0\rightarrow D^{*+}\pi^-$, the researchers derived an independent estimate of the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ lifetime. The result is 0.458$\pm$0.031 ps, offering a more precise determination of the lifetime despite the limited detection efficiency of the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay.

This study focuses on a specific control problem where the system's development is stochastic and occurs in discrete time. Given the limitations associated with applying traditional methods in this context, this examination uses a discretization approach to model the system's evolution within a semi-discrete framework, rather than a fully discrete one. This approach allows for the direct proof of the existence of optimal strategies, as well as their connection to a quasi-variational inequality, but requires the consideration of novel dissipation terms in the inequality and a specific regularity in its right-hand side, influenced by a discrete time component, in order to achieve the desired results. These developments contribute to the understanding of optimal control problems involving stochastic systems whose dynamics are subject to a discrete time framework.

Our analysis of high-energy observations from the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals an extensive pattern of variation in the direction of travel of recorded particles. An extensive parameter is defined as the cosine of the galactic coordinate of propagation of each recorded particle. A large dataset consisting of nearly 6 years of data above 4 EeV is analyzed to define a statistical measure of isotropy based on this definition. A noticeable decrease in this measure of isotropy as an increase in flux occurs can be attributed to both an increase in density of recorded particles near the Southern sky and difficulty in distinguishing between isotropic and anisotropic sources. Methods to account for this increase in density are discussed along with an estimation of anisotropic signals that could mislead into false positives. A straightforward approach to quantifying anisotropic components is explained. An increase in anisotropic components of 20% to 40% near the Southern sky is found and sources of anisotropy including an increase in composition of recorded particles and anisotropic components of an extragalactic flux can be discussed. Current data do not support a significant anisotropic flux above 4 EeV coming from the plane of the galaxy. Methods to account for sources of anisotropy can lead to a false increase in anisotropic components estimated near the Southern sky when assuming a mixed proton and heavy-nuclei flux. This study examines the capabilities of the ATLAS detector to measure the charge particle distribution and nuclear alteration factor in the interaction between protons and lead nuclei, with a focus on charged particle distribution in transverse momentum and forward rapidity, and comparative analysis in proton-proton and proton-lead interactions. The data with a focus on one-sided forward rapidity reveals an increased alteration factor for lower transverse momentum compared to higher, and more significant alteration in lead-lead interaction compared to proton-lead interaction, which contradicts previous findings from the CMS detector, and we discuss the source of this difference in measurement.

The study of hybrid C^*-dynamical systems, which incorporate both commuting and noncommuting elements, has been primarily conducted within the context of semisimple semidirect product Lie algebras. This research aims to expand this focus to include some nonsemisimple semidirect product Lie algebras. Within this investigation, specific commuting subalgebras and their corresponding dynamical behaviors are characterized, while also identifying cases where these behaviors exhibit stability under perturbation. These analyses lead to the development of new examples of Kadison-type and Arveson-type flows. Furthermore, certain algebraic structures are provided that facilitate further research into infinite dimensional semisimple Lie algebras.

A precise personalized therapy known as immune-checkpoint inhibition, targeted at cancer patients, relies on the categorization of tumor cells, specifically distinguishing between PD-L1 patients with tumors containing PD-L1 positive cells and those with PD-L1 negative tumors. However, effectively categorizing these cells demands training machine learning models on data from a vast number of hospitals due to the scarcity of annotated images. This model training process is complicated by the inability to share data between these institutions. Our research focuses on developing a federated learning approach to facilitate the training of classification models without exchanging data, instead, the models are trained by having each hospital train their own version and share only the updated knowledge with other participating institutions. We evaluated our method on data from four participating hospitals and found that it outperformed traditional learning techniques, resulting in a classification model with 71% accuracy.

Researchers have developed an innovative solution to a major issue that plagues underwater acoustic communication systems by creating a high-bandwidth, low-power decision feedback equalizer (DFE) suitable for use with nickel hydroxide batteries and small form factor modems. To make the compact DFE feasible, researchers designed novel methods to minimize the number of analog-to-digital converters needed and mitigated the mitigated the disruptive burst-errors that often occur within each modem symbol period. A novel equalization strategy was proposed, which effectively separates the burst-noise mitigation issue into two manageable sub-problems, allowing for precise equalizer coefficient estimation through a new filtering technique. A new model was also developed, which accurately captures the complex burst-error behavior, and enables performance prediction. A new equalization technique was proposed, which transforms the difficult problem of tracking fluctuating covariance matrices into a simpler and more manageable form, and allows for effective equalizer coefficient estimation. A new approach was proposed, which combines a robust sparse filter and a decision-directed sparse filter to achieve optimal equalization performance. To validate the effectiveness of this approach, Monte Carlo simulations were performed, which demonstrate the decision-directed DFE's superior robustness against the burst-error behavior and its consistent superiority over alternative decision-directed equalization techniques.

Recent advancements in temporal convolutional networks (TCNs) have made them a go-to choice for various time-series tasks. However, the design of TCNs poses a challenge due to its stacked structure, making it difficult to stretch or compress to meet different computational requirements. In contrast, TCNs can be resized using skip connections but struggle to maintain the stability of training across different sizes. On the other hand, TCNs with an all-stacked structure excel in performance but risk exceeding memory capacity when needed. TCNs with an all-trimmed structure are easy to size but may suffer from inefficient use of available resources. To address these challenges, we propose a new TCN design called Trimming In Time, which combines elements of both. "Trimming In Time" leverages a unique network optimization technique that adapts to specific resource requirements. Our experiments on multiple datasets and tasks show that TCNs with this approach outperform traditional designs while using fewer resources.

The paper proves that any finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra has a solvable lower central series, 
showing that all Zinbiel algebras are inherently solvable. It also provides a straightforward method to 
obtain this series and derives several related results, including the fact that Lie envelopes of Zinbiel 
algebras are also solvable. Furthermore, the document establishes that finite-dimensional nil Zinbiel 
algebras are finite-dimensional nil Lie algebras with a corresponding nil Lie envelope.

Our investigation involves an analysis of the one-dimensional entropy spectra to examine the one-dimensional entropic density variations as a function of displacement in the direction of flow within the Pb-Pb collisions at the LHC, conducted at an energy level of 5.02 TeV and an interaction luminosity of 4.5 millibarns per second. The data collected corresponds to specific centrality intervals, namely 0-5%, 10-15%, 20-25%, 30-35%, 40-45%, 45-50%, 50-55%, 55-60%, 60-65%, 65-70%, 70-75%, 75-80%, 80-85%, 85-90%, 90-95%, and 5.01 TeV Pb-Pb collisions. The findings reveal an increase in the one-dimensional entropy density from the initial more peripheral collisions towards the more central collisions, accompanied by a corresponding increase in the mean radius from the initial more peripheral collisions towards the more central collisions, thus supporting hadronization theory. Moreover, the linear regression line derived from the data shows that the entropy variations follow a linear progression in accordance with the variations in the mean radius in the direction of flow, supporting the hadronization theory. The concept of local entailment was first introduced by A. Carro and F. Esteva in 2009 to effectively manage formulas within the framework of the three-valued logic system N3. This framework was later generalized by A. Galato, R. Horita, and T. Uchino in 2013 to encompass an arbitrary language containing a distinguished set of formulas representing entailment. Since its introduction, the framework of endo-preliminary local entailments (EPLs) has been applied to various logic systems, including the logic systems of relevantly and substructurally. However, the local nature of EPLs restricts import-exponentiation and co-Kleisli adjunction to be defined only after eliminating a specific variable. To address this limitation, the notion of local entailment with dummy variables was proposed to expand the scope of local entailments beyond traditional logic systems. This proposal also enables the definition of unified inverse relations that preserve adjunction in a manner consistent with the endo-preliminary framework.

Deterministic functional dependencies are a crucial concept in table analysis, with applications in database design, data mining, and cleaning. However, employing non-deterministic dependencies on flawed, incomplete tables presents significant challenges due to potential ambiguity and conflict. This paper aims to address this challenge by formulating conflict-resolution procedures that acknowledge determinism violations. We investigate two critical questions: how to mathematically model conflict resolution, and how to efficiently compute solutions. In doing so, we focus on tables with missing data and explore the complexities of applying conflict-determined dependencies. Notably, we identify the computational difficulty of these problems, and investigate the impact of additional dependencies, such as acyclic ones. Finally, we apply our findings to the problem of table generalization, and propose methods for solving real-world problems, such as handling conflicting file encodings.

This paper presents an initial framework for a new statistical model called Temporal-Varying Poisson Autoregressive Model. We derive the model's likelihood function and employ a Gibbs sampler to sample from the posterior distribution of model parameters. A specific application is used to illustrate the model, from which we also conduct a simulation study. Furthermore, we utilize a real dataset to demonstrate the model's capabilities, specifically using data on the number of best-selling songs in Japan from 2004 to 2014.

This paper introduces Neural Description Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation method, to solve complex robotic tasks involving unstructured parts. Parts are often irregular and lack inherent features, which can hinder straightforward description. We address this issue by representing 3D point clouds as joint probability distributions over description variables, such as angles and distances, relative to planar cross-section slices. Our approach extracts a consistent description from various object viewpoints, allowing for reliable extraction and interpretation by planners or controllers. In robotic experiments, we demonstrate our method's effectiveness in achieving reliable descriptions, accurate fit, and precise placement, even when points clouds are incomplete or viewed from different angles.

The initial SiD design is now being modified, considering the impact of a modified silicon thickness and the use of thinner gaps between layers on tracking performance, with a specific focus on inner radius variants and gap reductions, as well as material characteristics such as interaction lengths and point resolution.

We examined the stellar composition of the globular cluster NGC 5898 using a comprehensive analysis of multi-dimensional spectroscopy, based on observations from the APOgee survey of the Tonantzintla 2 field. By combining high-resolution spectra from GAIL and external catalogues of optical photometry and astrometry, we created a robust sample of galaxies within 6 kiloparsecs. Our team used machine learning techniques to classify each stellar spectrum, and we discovered that most of the stars within our sample belong to the galactic bulge, although some belong to the thin disk. By comparing the spectral features of the bulge stars to those of the globular cluster, we found that they share very similar properties in terms of metallicity, abundance spread, surface gravity, and rotation. Specifically, their metallicity, $[Fe/H]$, is $-0.50 \pm 0.07$ dex, and their spread, $\Delta[Fe/H]$, is $0.34 \pm 0.07$ dex. Their surface rotation velocity is $-23.3 \pm 0.9$ km/s, and their asymptotic giant branch morphology suggests that they may be influenced by the same forces that affect other bulge stars. These findings suggest that the formation history of the globular cluster shares similarities with that of the general bulge population.

The proliferation of formally verified mathematical theories, compiled in the Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs, signifies the success of the Isabelle community. To facilitate rapid access to these achievements, a structure called the Framework in Theorem Demonstration is proposed. This proposed framework consists of three core components: a core library containing foundational and modular building blocks, derived libraries derived from the core library to address more complex proofs, and a comprehensive index connecting all frameworks. To promote the development of this framework, three pivotal questions are posed to guide the Isabelle community in the advancement of the framework.

This study seeks to identify the position of the Yang-Lee edge singularity within the critical region of the $d$-dimensional, ferromagnetic, $d$-spin model under the influence of a magnetic field. Analysis was performed using field theory and was then verified by conducting Monte Carlo simulations in dimensions 2, 3, and 3.5, utilizing various traditional $O(N)$ spin models including $O(2)$, $O(3)$, and $O(4}$ for a 2-dimensional square lattice, an $O(3)$ model based on a 3-dimensional cubic lattice, and for 3.5-dimensional critical behavior using the finite scaling method. Our research indicates that the critical dimension $d_c$ for the Yang-Lee edge singularity is between 1.9125 and 1.96 for the $O(2)$ Ising model, lies between 2.01 and 2.07 for the $O(3)$ model, and is situated between 2.46 and 2.57 for $O(4)$, with an implication that it may not be found in any 2-dimensional traditional $O(N)$ spin model underlying the critical point of the Yang-Lee edge singularity lies between the critical dimensions of the $O(2)$ and $O(4)$ models.

In high-dimensional statistics and machine learning, it is essential to establish the local convexity of objective functions within wide neighborhoods of optimal solutions, an approach known as "local strong convexity." The "Sudakov-Fernique" principle, a powerful tool, enables the expectation preservation of monotonic functions, and we leverage it to provide an expectation argument for proving the local convexity of the TAP free energy, a key component in understanding Bayesian inference for planted sparse recovery and tensor PCA. This expectation argument allows us to prove that its projection onto the space of diagonal matrices is locally convex around the optimal solution, and we demonstrate how this result can be applied to prove a version of the "non-rigorous" local convexity of the TAP free energy. Our work also reveals a deeper significance of the "replica symmetry breaking" phenomenon in relation to phase transitions of condensation and shows how an alternative, simpler proof of a specific result is achievable.

This computational examination provides practical guidance for researchers
investigating metasurfaces, which are materials with unique properties due to
their two-dimensional nature. Given their potential to alter physical phenomena
at their boundaries, metasurfaces have garnered substantial interest in the
scientific community. However, formulating three-dimensional problems based on
specific desired two-dimensional effects can be a challenging task. We present an
efficient computational framework to realize various one, two, or three-dimensional
planar prototypes, examining their distinctive properties in simulated scenarios.
Our code utilizes open-source components and can be easily adapted for other
situations, resulting in a cost-effective and scalable examination of metasurfaces.

The primary objective of this research is to verify the conjugation of a given smooth vector field near a hyperbolic periodic orbit. Specifically, it can be transformed into a vector field with a periodic orbit that maintains stability. The proof of this conjugation relies on established methods of orbital linearization. These methods are reviewed and summarized in this study, which also presents original results concerning smooth totally integrable vector fields. In a given open subset of the phase space, such a field can be expressed as a smooth rescaling of a field with a degenerate first integral possessing a nonvanishing derivative. This rescaling involves the product of a given smooth function with a smooth vector field with an isolated singularity. This finding is then applied to confirm the orbital linearization of supermultipoles presented in a recent publication.

This study proposes a unique deep learning approach to solve the configuration interaction problem in quantum chemistry. The model is trained to predict the ground state energy of a system by inputting the electronic configuration. Surprisingly, it discovers that a single neural network is sufficient for this prediction. The implementation is efficient and versatile, capable of handling different bases and nuclear configurations, and is tested for accuracy across a range of challenging quantum chemistry problems. The results are competitive with the best existing methods and the model is also used to investigate complex electronic states in helium, lithium beryllium and neon atoms. Additionally, a neural network approach is efficient in determining the complete configuration interaction ground and low-lying excited state spectra for water in a $[10s6p5d]/[6s4p3d]$ basis and in combination with a stochastic method for flexible bases. The findings show a minimal loss in accuracy and reduce the computational cost by a significant margin.

The Waltzer's massive elliptical arc, first noticed in the Chandra Deepck2 survey, is a notable discovery. Located in the constellation of the Centaurus, it spans nearly half a degree and encompasses over ten million suns. To investigate its properties, we compiled and analyzed X-ray data from multiple surveys, allowing for precise positional determination of X-ray sources. Through this analysis, we established the arc's true shape, orientation, and estimated mass of its contents. We explored several hypotheses regarding its origin, such as a chance alignment of a spiral arm, the remnant of a disrupted bar from a merging galaxy, or the result of a gas interaction during a major galaxy merger event. However, none of these hypotheses fully explained the observed features. We propose an alternative explanation: the arc may be the product of a tidal interaction between two gas-rich galaxies that produced a distinctive double-arc structure, as seen in the nearby Southern Cluster. Further observations are required to confirm this theory.

The precise measurement of astrophysical signals hindered by atmospheric scattering and the development of accurate methods to mitigate atmospheric effects are crucial for the successful outcome of upcoming Extremely Large Telescopes. Due to the night sky's brightness, the significant amount of photons that can be collected, even from a single star, results in the noise being dominated by that from the detector rather than the variation in the number of photons that reach the telescope from a stellar source, which is heavily influenced by the presence of aerosols in the atmosphere. This document will present cutting-edge detector technology, analyze the sources of noise in modern detectors, and provide equations and methods for the most accurate possible measurements of the atmospheric transmission using the photometric data. Through the most precise possible measurements of the atmospheric transmission using the photometric data, we can derive highly accurate estimates of the aerosol optical depth and the size distribution of the aerosols from the atmosphere.

This paper proposes a novel end-to-end pose estimation method for objects with six degrees of freedom based on a single 2D image. To enhance pose estimation accuracy, particularly for rolling and rotating motions, this paper introduces two innovations: first, modifying the convolutional projection network to group pixels by correspondence, creating enhanced hierarchical correspondence maps; second, integrating a clustering projection network in the loss function to implicitly project depth estimates onto the 3D shape of the object. These innovations allow the object's position, orientation, and depth to be accurately determined from a single image. By optimizing the object's six degrees of freedom through pose loss and photometric loss, precise pose estimation becomes possible. Our method outperforms existing techniques, achieving state-of-the-art results on multiple benchmarks including the NYUv2 dataset and the HM3D pose validation set. Source code is available online at this link: https://github.com/ChengShi2017/DeepHMap-.

Nonlocal integral theories have gained significant importance in modeling materials with unpredictable and localized failure behavior. This has sparked a diverse range of nonlocal models, but their mathematical and physical complexities have hindered model comparisons and evaluations. This review paper explores nonlocal integral theories of fluid mechanics, examining recent developments across various models despite their limitations. Although these developments have promising applications, their theoretical complexities have not been fully resolved, posing challenges for model comparisons and assessments within the field of fluid mechanics.

Graphical Lasso algorithms are commonly used in analyzing large datasets, such as in neuroscience, to infer connections between a given set of variables, for example, neural nodes. To efficiently carry out this analysis on large datasets, specialized software implementations are necessary. The GGLasso is a new Python library designed to facilitate Graphical Lasso calculations, supporting both CPU and GPU processing through integration with Numba and CuItu. GGLasso includes methods for sparse matrix operations, eigenvalue decomposition, and is accompanied by extensive documentation and test cases to assist users in adapting it to their specific projects.

Designing molecules with complex 3D molecular shapes is a common task in chemistry and material science that often relies on computational techniques to visualize and analyze their molecular structures. Configurational optimization is one such approach, where configurations are gradually adjusted to reach a target energy state, but this optimization can be sensitive to initial conditions and prone to getting stuck in local solutions. In this paper, we investigate the use of Langevin dynamics for configuring molecular configurations and present two evaluation metrics to assess their performance, including a newly developed metric called Distortion that complements the widely used RMSD metric. We also demonstrate the effectiveness of Langevin dynamics in sampling configurational molecules through multiple test cases, from simple water molecules to complex proteins, showing its ability to consistently produce high-quality configurations with low errors in comparison to reference configurations, outperforming the commonly used configurational optimization technique.

This research builds upon a previously developed model describing the interaction between accreting flows and electromagnetic waves/excessive radiation surrounding certain astrophysical compact objects. According to this model, an area known as the "wave shadow" emerges where the gravitational field of the compact object is strong enough to capture waves, appearing as a dark disk surrounding the object. The study simulates how black hole mergers interact with matter "wave shadow" regions using general relativistic hydrodynamics simulations. These simulations are performed for various scenarios involving supermassive black holes merging with stellar-mass black holes in different masses and spins, as well as their surrounding "wave shadow" regions. The simulations investigate the behavior of matter within wave shadow regions before, during, and after the merger event, and reveal how the characteristic "wave shadow" shapes and sizes affect the appearance of the merger event, often producing distinctive features such as bright halos and tidal streams of accreting matter.

Consider an extended Euler-Bernoulli beam consisting of a main beam connected to $N$ additional sub-beams at its vertices, where the connections form a tree structure. This setup forms an $(N+1)$-star graph. Using the method of multiplier laws, we analyze how small vibrations propagate through this system. It is demonstrated that under specific geometric conditions, the spectrum of this dynamical system exhibits an eigenvalue accumulation point at infinity, exhibiting square-root spacing. Consequently, the spectrum contains both discrete and continuous components, with the continuous part starting from this infinite eigenvalue point. Furthermore, all eigenfunctions corresponding to bounded eigenvalues are located within the main beam, whereas those corresponding to functions representing the interval $(\rho, \infty)$ are found exclusively in the auxiliary beams and not in the main beam. Thus, the extended beam exhibits complete vibrational dislocation. Key geometric parameters influencing $\rho$ include the measure of angle at the junction points, the degree of these points, and the internal friction characteristics of the beam.
