For any symplectic map from a tiny neighborhood of a fixed point on a torus $T^2$ to another symplectic manifold, we determine the symplectic homotopy classes associated with the category theory of its pullback diagrams. By utilizing these 'symplectic $n$-categories', we can then investigate the structural properties of the symplectic mapping theories of various symplectic manifolds, particularly in relation to their relationship with blowups of a torus.

This paper provides a proof of a previously unestablished instance of irregular Nambu-Goldstone theorem within the frameworks of relativistic and nonrelativistic quantum field theory. A key feature of our proof involves the utilization of the independent infinitesimal transformation property of the canonical commutation (or anti-commutation) relations (CCR/(A)) by employing a specific class of well-behaved vectors known as a dense nuclear subspace of the Hilbert space. The ultimate application of our findings relates to quantum chromodynamics, particularly in proving the continuous symmetry breaking of the vacuum in this theory. Our demonstration relies on the utilization of Glimm-Jaffe's established facts and rigorous nonperturbative results, derived from the axiomatic approach to quantum field theory, specifically the Maumin-Kadant-Simon (MKS) approach and the axiomatic theory developed by Streater-Wight (SW). A significant aspect of our approach utilizes the rigorous, nonperturbative results derived within the axiomatic theory, rather than relying on formal or Lagrangian-based approaches. A crucial application of our findings provides a rigorous derivation of the vacuum expectation value of the quark mass within quantum chromodynamics, utilizing the nonperturbative results derived within the axiomatic theory, specifically regarding the constituent quark mass, partial chiral symmetry breaking, and the associated pole of the scalar quark propagator. Our approach also relates to the distinct constituent quark mass in quantum chromodynamics, derived

Current natural language processing NLP models excel at word-level counterfactual analysis but fall short in capturing complex, phrasal counterfactuals necessary for a more accurate evaluation of NLP NLU components. A new algorithm is introduced, DISCO, which can extract a wide range of counterfactual sentences from data sets, covering both simple and complex, word-level and multi-word cases. Experimental results show that applying this method can uncover a broad spectrum of counterfactuals with a high level of feasibility. Furthermore, findings indicate that the extracted data sets can effectively critique the performance of core NLP NLU models across eight distinct tasks. As a result, this method provides a robust and reliable tool for evaluating the counterfactual capabilities of NLP models across multiple natural language understanding tasks.

The total coloring conjecture posits that every connected graph G with maximum degree Δ requires a specific number of edges to be colored in a particular way. A graph is considered fair total colorable if it can be colored in this way using 2Δ - 1 colors. Previous research has established that certain types of root-colored graphs are (2Δ - 1) colorable or at least have a high chromatic index close to 2Δ. This paper aims to (2Δ - 1) color several types of circulant graphs, including double stars, and demonstrate the feasibility of coloring them with an adequate number of colors to maintain a certain color distinction.

In our investigation, we used first-principles calculations to study the growth of cubic Heusler alloys like CoNiSn, Co2MnSn, and Cu2MnSn on an octahedral or rhombohedral graphene layer seated on a sapphire substrate. We found that when these alloys bond directly to the underlying graphene, they follow a specific epitaxial relationship. However, adding a thin oxide layer between the graphene and the alloys shifts them to grow in an unconventional manner. By analyzing their lattice misfit, we found that Cu2Mnsn grows in two distinct phases, while CoNiSn and Co2MnSn maintain stability. Furthermore, we explored how a wedge-shaped variation in thickness affects their elasticity and stress, and discovered that Heusler layers will switch between direct bonding and a gap-opening scenario based on a critical thickness determined by a van der Waals force. This research deepens our understanding of the complex forces at play during the growth of these materials and is essential for producing high-quality films used in spintronics applications.

This paper examines the rank and $\Lambda$-null space dimension of codes that are linear in the sense of $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$. We derive formulas for the rank when $p$ is equal to 2 or greater than 3, as well as the null space dimension for both types of codes. We also determine the rank and null space dimension for a few specific codes, the [2,1,3]$_\mathbb{Z}_4\mathbb{Z}_9$-code, the [$2n$,$n$,6]$_\mathbb{Z}_4\mathbb{Z}_9$-code family, and the [10,5,10]$_\mathbb{Z}_4\mathbb{Z}_9$-code, the latter being a optimal code in the sense of $\mathbb{Z}_4\mathbb{Z}_9$-linearity.

In the oil industry, a well-established technique for enhancing recovery rates involves the injection of polymer slugs, yet its full potential remains untapped due to the technique's limited adoption. Presently, most research focuses on evaluating various polymer injection methods under uniform flow conditions in a laboratory setting. In contrast, our work aims to investigate how the method of polymer injection impacts flow dynamics and ultimate oil recovery in a fractured reservoir, utilizing the SPE10 benchmark model. Our findings highlight that altering polymer slug insertion methods can significantly influence oil production outcomes, with certain patterns yielding up to 25% more oil than others. Notably, patterns that promote early channel formation near the wellbore in the matrix rock tend to reduce oil production, whereas patterns concentrating the polymer near a fracture surface facilitate optimal oil recovery. Ultimately, our study emphasizes the necessity of numerically optimizing polymer slug insertion patterns to maximize oil production in fractured reservoirs.

The scarcity of data that simultaneously labels multiple concepts within a single entry frequently necessitates utilizing datasets where distinct entries bear singular labels. To circumvent this issue, a common approach involves creating artificial entries based on existing ones with individual labels. Yet, this technique often generates entries of poor quality due to the lack of guarantee that combining the individual labels accurately reflects their combined frequency. An alternative strategy proposes selecting only high-quality pairings from all possible combinations of existing single-labeled entries, but this demands an extensive, unattainable dataset. In contrast, our proposed framework extracts reliable multi-concept labels from single-concept entries with existing data. In contrast to existing methods that rely on probabilistic models, our algorithm produces direct output suitable for machine learning models. Experimental evidence demonstrates the superiority of our method over existing techniques across various tasks and datasets.

For a variety of phenomena, including crystalline growth and phase-field dynamics described by the time-fractional Cahn-Lasek and Hele-Shaw equations, an unusual upper bound on energy evolution over time has been conjectured. A corresponding hypothesis stated that the energy at any given time $t$ would not surpass the initial energy multiplied by the time $t$ raised to the power of $1-\alpha$, where $\alpha$ is an exponent reflecting anomalous, memory-dependent diffusion rates and is found within the interval $(0,1)$. Our numerical experiments utilizing a novel, unstructured-grid-based method have confirmed this upper limit across different scenarios corresponding to Cahn-Lasker, Hele-Shaw and MFPP equations. Furthermore, our findings indicate the exponent $1-\alpha$ varies systematically, whereas alternative approaches, which model the rate of time as $t^{2n-1}$, result in energy violations when employing the higher-order method and are found inconsistent.

The construction of a Hilbert space from a given set of physical quantities and possible configurations of a system constitutes a fundamental step in developing a quantum theory. This process can be understood as an example of a broader relationship, a kind of adjunction, that characterizes Hilbert spaces and their associated physical properties and configurations within the framework of a 2-categorical structure. Furthermore, this adjunction has a dual counterpart that allows for the derivation of physical quantities and configurations from a provided Hilbert space, within the same 2-categorical structure.

We develop a new theory to explain high-energy gamma-rays found in nearby radio galaxies and quasars at energy levels above 1 GeV. This theory involves interacting turbulent magnetic fields in the accretion disk of these galaxies, and suggests that gamma-rays are generated by energetic particles trapped in these magnetic fields within a wide area surrounding the accretion disk. In contrast to previously proposed models, our model doesn't require detecting active jets but does predict that high-energy gamma-rays should be found in galaxies with only slow-energy output. This is confirmed by observations that show a significant gamma-ray flux in some galaxy without a detectable radio output. This discrepancy cannot be accounted for by standard models of galaxy activity. However, the theoretical maximum energy of particles in our model aligns with the energy levels observed in gamma-rays.

This paper presents an advanced optimization approach to enhance the dispersion of a portfolio's yield across its width, using a novel term added to the objective function. The new term is grounded in order-weighted absolute deviation concepts and is formulated as a mixed-integer linear program for efficiency. The proposed approach is part of a broader framework known as the dispersion maximization portfolio selection model, an alternative to the widely-used diversification maximization model. The efficiency and practical application of the proposed optimization term are demonstrated through numerical experiments, utilizing the EMOA-Dispersion portfolio selection model as a platform for optimization.

This research paper focuses on developing a method to classify heart sounds, which can signify various conditions including normal heart function and the presence of pathologies like mitral valve stenosis, using non-contact data obtained through near-infrared spectroscopy. To acquire this data, the authors employed a device that records skin surface changes caused by cardiac activity after processing for arterial tonometry. Due to the signal's small magnitude and possible distortion from filtering and external factors, traditional classification approaches face challenges. To overcome these, the researchers developed a combination of a machine learning method, specifically support vector machines, and a neural network called a variational autoencoder to efficiently classify signals representing normal heart function and pathology. This combination enabled them to effectively classify the signals with an accuracy of 98.5%.

The proliferation of smartphones, smartphones, and wearable technology has made it possible for users to generate massive amounts of health data through various electronic health tools. This has led to the development of machine learning models that can make accurate health predictions, such as activity recognition and activity prediction based on past patterns. However, there are significant obstacles to training these models using raw data, primarily concerns over data privacy and security. As an alternative, federated learning enables collaborative model optimization without the need to share raw data with external entities. This paper outlines the federated transfer learning architecture FedHealth, which employs a unique knowledge graph structure to facilitate collaboration among users and enables the exchange of valuable data insights in a private manner. Experimental evaluations demonstrate the effectiveness of FedHealth in accurately recognizing activities and predicting them in various scenarios, outperforming traditional ensemble methods based on federated learning.

This paper belongs to the technique section and investigates connections between various portfolio optimization methods centered on higher-order moment superiority. At the core of this research is the argument that traditional quadratic mean-variance analysis represents a fundamental component of superiority-based methods. Moreover, these techniques, which focus on higher-order moments, generally build upon the fundamental concepts of mean-variance understanding. The paper begins by categorizing superiority-based methods based on their underlying approaches, rather than their mathematical formulations. The reviewed methods include those that prioritize goal programming, composite optimization, and fuzzy logic, all of which take into account the preferences and desires of their decision-makers. The discussion then shifts to a specific application within the Iranian financial market, where an aggregated approach is employed to satisfy the priority-based constraints of goal programming, data envelopment analysis (DEA), fuzzy logic, and superiority moment techniques. The paper concludes with a critical analysis of the methods, highlighting their respective strengths and weaknesses, as well as recommendations for future research directions.

The discrepancy between the predicted abundance of dark matter and the observed amounts in galaxy cores versus the early universe is the 2Hc problem. We suggest that sub-KeV sterile neutrinos could resolve this issue, and through a specific string theory mechanism, we derive their appropriate abundance. This solution allows us to match the early universe's dark matter density, but we find that cold dark matter models fail to explain the dark matter distribution in galaxy cores. In contrast, we demonstrate that warm dark matter arising from sterile neutrinos aligns with both dark matter abundance and spatial distribution findings.

This paper presents an automated method to facilitate software users with various disabilities, specifically those who are deaf, blind, or have limited vision. Our approach involves creating an automatic system that generates custom software interfaces, providing accessible versions for screen readers, visual alert indicators, and text-based communication platforms. We automate the conversion process and conducted experiments using three pairs of regular and accessible interfaces to collect and analyze data on software perception, recognition, and learning among participants with visual or sight-impaired conditions. Our research results, including relevant metrics and reasoning, are included in the report to establish a solid foundation for future studies in this field.

This paper addresses the minimum cost control problem toggle type under a specific constraint, where an operational decision, determined by the process's state, must at some point switch to its opposite within the given time frame. The problem's variant discussed here aligns with a common model used in option pricing, but features a unique cost structure that changes at a rapid rate and with abrupt jumps. The study involves the development of a value function that satisfies an elaborate/capitated variation of the probabilistic camouflaged Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman-Isaacs equation, whose solution is the fundamental solution to this problem's control issue. The provided control is basic under a specific definition and can be proven through the application of a verification theorem. The theorem's proof, however, requires the establishment of the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman-Isaacs equation's unique causal, regularized semimartingale solution, and ultimately, the solution to this problem. The proof of the verification theorem, in turn, relies heavily on the preceding result.

This paper explores a new scenario for leptoquark production where a pair of different types of leptoquarks are created through the interaction of gluons via the addition of a Higgs boson's interaction. To investigate this, even so-called type II leptoquarks were studied within the context of the Color-Flavor-Locked (CFL) neutron star phase. Since neutron stars contain large amounts of quarks and gluons, their interaction with type II leptoquarks could result in the emission of different types of leptoquarks and their opposite partners. If this occurs, it may be possible to detect distinct signals from quark matter in the Colliders at the Large Hadron Collider. Furthermore, this paper also considers the impact of this scenario on the stability of the CFL phase and suggests modifications to the equation of state that could be detected through gravitational wave observations.

In life sciences, temporal series analysis is often complicated by small sample sizes and unknown dimensionality. These factors hinder the application of supervised learning techniques. To circumvent this limitation, we propose a learning algorithm based on a directed graph called Monitored Learning of Temporal Series (MLTS). This algorithm can learn the dimensionality and structure of high-dimensional data without a test set. By employing graph-based representations and an optimization criterion, MLTS allows for the comparison of different models and selection of the best one that generalizes well to unseen data. We demonstrate the benefits of MLTS by using it to model the transmission of SARS-CoV-2 transmission in Italy, showing that it outperforms other graph-based models and provides a more accurate and efficient representation of the data.

Photodissociation regions, heated by young stars, typically exhibit temperatures between -30 and -50, making them ideal for molecular hydrogen emission lines that are often too faint for precise temperature measurement. As a result, the exact temperature of this gas remains largely unknown. However, the lines of molecular cyanide can be utilized to accurately temperature gauge this gas. Conversely, molecular gas reservoirs, not subjected to young star heating, are instead illuminated by distant galaxies' ultraviolet light. This creates molecular cyanide lines that are significantly narrower and pose challenges in detection. Nevertheless, recent observations have managed to temperature measure these lines, revealing a broad spectrum of temperatures, including the molecular gas reservoir temperatures.

In a novel theory where the Higgs boson is a composite entity, the exact nature of fermions that interact with it is determined by the relative timing of their own composite formation in comparison to that of the scale $\Lambda$.  In this scenario, the lightest fermions, the Higgs being a bound state of two fermionic constituents, would already be composite at energies lower than $\Lambda$, resulting in a distinctive pattern of electroweak symmetry breaking violations, specifically with $K$ dominance and $K \gg B$, with possible contributions from other terms such as $f$, $g$, $g_L$, and $g_R$.  On the other hand, heavier fermions, which become composite at or above $\Lambda$, give rise to the dominant $B$ irregularity, specifically with $B \gg K$, essentially meaning that the $B$ term is where most of the Higgs physics lies, with relatively minor contributions from other terms including $K$, with possible dominance of other terms such as $f$, $g$, $g_L$, and $g_R$.  In this paper, we map out both regions with $K$ and $B$ dominance within the broader context of their respective relationships, and we suggest that a more in-depth theoretical investigation is needed to better understand and describe these two distinct but complementary scenarios.  In particular, we note that the region of $K$ dominance essentially translates to the framework of traditional composite Higgs models, and

Given scores $s_\tau(x)$ associated with pairs of elements for an ordered set $\tau(\mathcal{X})$, our objective is to determine the corresponding order $\tau(\mathcal{X})$. This problem is prevalent in machine learning applications such as list prediction, where the output is a sequence rather than a single element or a partial order. We examine the series reconstruction challenge for permutations using the Hamming divergence metric. Under specific conditions, we have discovered that an episodic approach outperforms a global method in minimizing these errors. Furthermore, we have compared both approaches and obtained results. Our experiments reveal that the optimal strategy involves a non-intuitive combination of Gaussian regression and binarization. Compared to a direct method that aims to hamming-project onto the target permutation, our series reconstruction approach has shown a significant improvement of 21% in mean absolute error through both synthetic and empirical evaluations.

Despite the progress in identifying everyday objects through pattern recognition, the task of identifying musical instruments remains largely underexplored in the field of computer vision research. Current pattern recognition approaches often depend on large labeled datasets, making them inefficient and costly to utilize. To overcome this limitation, we investigate the implementation of few-shot learning techniques for the identification of musical instruments. We present a two-tiered hierarchical hierarchical framework consisting of a coarse-grained and a fine-grained classification framework. Initially, the system performs a general classification to distinguish between musicians and non-musicians, and then proceeds to a detailed analysis to identify specific instruments within the musical category. We adapt the hierarchical framework from the Food-101 dataset and evaluate its performance in a few-shot learning context. Our results indicate substantial enhancements in accuracy compared to existing methods, and the system's capacity to operate with limited labeled data makes it cost-effective and cost-efficient to deploy.

We have put together a comprehensive collection of pinpointed, information-driven spots within scholarly papers, derived from the general public's curiosity on topics such as NLP, ML, and CL through Google Queries. If possible, we also provided answers to these queries based on the content of the associated research papers. This meaningful, knowledge-oriented dataset can serve as a valuable resource for advancing the capabilities of information-focused systems and potentially serve as a testing ground for the public's perception and trust in these systems. It has been made openly available at http://www.parkerlab.org/kcqa/.

We have developed an automated method to generate precise waveforms for merging pulsar timing array signals from eccentric binary systems using general relativity corrections in a post-Newtonian framework. These systems emit continuous waves that scan over sky paths and produce characteristic chirps as they merge. Our method involves a high-efficiency algorithm that: (1) obtains merger times and orientations through sky rotations, and and and (2) calculates weighted probabilities of observed PA configurations by solving a high-dimensional integral. We determine the precision and runtime of this algorithm for various waveform characteristics using merging eccentric binaries as examples, and calculate the number of pixels required to detect PA characteristics with sufficient significance. Additionally, we derive an efficient method to detect mergers from semi-parametric continuous waves using this algorithm, and it is found that General Relativistic resonances can provide sufficient information to constrain waveform parameters and merging characteristics, and calculate the minimum number of pulsars needed to detect these features with a high degree of confidence, and and and (5) calculate the minimum number of pulsars needed to detect this feature with a high degree of confidence.

To analyze high-speed asymmetric simple exclusion processes, we examine a system of particles following ASEP under Poincaré's expansion, where one lane is significantly slower than the others. Our research reveals detailed velocity adjustments across three distinct speed-regime categories. Among these, we can reconstruct the slower lane's density from the faster lanes' densities in a moderate regime. Additionally, this moderate regime is linked to Tolocci-Toscani's reconnection phenomenon.

As the ongoing epidemic progresses, governments and health organizations are gathering more data and insights into its transmission dynamics, a situation that is creating an opportunity to explore and analyze the mathematical models being used to model its spread.

Multiple mathematical models have been developed and applied to understand infectious diseases, a situation that is causing confusion among non-experts due to varying results and interpretations. In this context, we aim to provide an opportunity for readers to review and analyze key mathematical models that have been published and discussed in the scientific literature.

In this paper, we explore and explain key mathematical models that have been used to model outbreaks and infectious diseases, a opportunity that is provided by the ongoing epidemic. In this context, we discuss stochastic and deterministic approaches to understanding the early stages of an outbreak, a situation that is further explored by analyzing simple SIR models through both stochastic and deterministic frameworks. In this context, we also examine the application of these mathematical models to real-world data and potential future research opportunities for bracketing estimates of key epidemic parameters.

This analysis of Majorana particles reveals their distribution follows a unique pattern,  
which can be described as an modified Gaussian distribution centered at zero. This  
characteristic is distinct from both bosons and fermions located in distinct states. As  
such, we propose a measure of entanglement that leverages this pattern. Furthermore,  
we suggest that the pattern's formation is due to the anti-unitary nature of Majorana  
symmetry. This explanation applies to all systems exhibiting Majorana symmetry,  
including some topological superconductors capable of generating a pattern identical  
to the one described.

Acronyms serve as a lexical phenomenon that saves space but poses a lexical gap, requiring readers to resolve them to fully comprehend the text. This resolution process is more intricate than understanding non-abridged words due to the one-to-many mapping between an anagram and its potential expansions. In the past decade, the surge of English content on the internet has created environments rife with informal language and multiple layers of meaning, making acronym resolution even more challenging. To address this challenge, we introduce an online platform called MadDog, which provides acronyms from informal English sources with their intended meanings. This platform is unique in offering a comprehensive set of tools for identifying and investigating acronyms, including: (i) ANI-based identification, which leverages ANagrams Indicators to identify potential anagrams, (ii) a user-friendly interface for user-contributed submissions, (iii) ANI-enhanced search to find anagrams with their potential expansions, and (iv) acronyms' metadata management, which acquires acronyms' metadata from online sources, including origin, age, and popularity. As far as we know, this platform is the first of its kind to provide comprehensive acronyms and their metadata from informal English content on the internet.

Recently, a significant transformation was observed in alkali metal dimers, where large entities evolved into small ones, specifically in areas of $^1$S $^1$Na$_2$ with very high binding energy and it occurred as a result of bosonic dimers becoming unstable and dissociating into sparse alkaline atoms. In contrast, a recent study has revealed an unexpected phenomenon in which pairs of fermionic Rb atoms could form weakly bound dimers that exhibited molecule- like properties, despite being impossible for homonuclear Rb$_2$ molecules to exist in a fermionic state. These molecules were actually composed of opposite-spin atoms and were made possible by extremely high resonance conditions, as well as a complex interaction between two opposite-spin boson and fermion components. A semi-analytical approach has provided insight into this molecular spectrum and identified a region where fermiboson dimers could transform into molecule resonances. A prediction was also made regarding the possibility of inducing a transformation from spinor particles to particles composed of two particles, by altering the relative intensity of interactions and adjusting the number of laser photons used in a three-body process involving two counter-propagating circularly polarized lasers system.

Despite its high storage capacity and fast retrieval speed, DNA storage still faces challenges in areas like storage cost, error rate, and hierarchy and dynamic information update management. A new method is proposed to address these issues, drawing from the human memory system's hierarchy and update system. A new encoding method called Hierarchy and Information Update (HIU) encoding is proposed, which uses unique markers to denote different information levels and employs a shifting method to update or delete information. Two variations of the HIU encoding method are proposed and analyzed, with theoretical and practical results showing significant improvements in code rate, rate loss, and error correction capability compared to existing encoding methods.

Recent topological research has focused on momentum spacetime structures, particularly on dual manifolds with three dimensions separated by nodal surfaces. These nodal surfaces represent a distinct type of symmetry-protected degeneracy that defines the boundary between distinct topological phases characterized by unique surface anomaly invariants. Current studies have now started to explore realizations of such nodal surfaces across various systems, including semimetals with distinct magnetic properties and metalloids, as well as photonic implementations using waveguide and photonic crystal slabs. This paper provides now an overview of the fundamental characteristics of these nodal surfaces, including their topological properties and mathematical description through the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ invariant computation, and discusses their manifestation in the aforementioned systems.

A brain tumor is a malignant growth that develops within the brain and can affect anyone, regardless of age. The precise diagnosis and treatment of brain tumors rely heavily on accurate detection and classification. Using deep learning techniques, researchers have made significant strides in automating the detection and classification of tumors in magnetic resonance images. However, most existing methods only address either detection or classification, ignoring the potential for a unified approach. To tackle this challenge, we present a novel end-to-end network called Multi-task focus directed network for brain tumor delineation and categorization, which simultaneously deals with detection and classification. Our method leverages a dual-task framework, where a segmentation task informs a classification task and vice versa, allowing for a more accurate and efficient outcome. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of our approach over state-of-the-art methods on two widely used datasets, NMIA and TUMOR-PHENOTYPE.

We introduce an innovative method for calculating shadow calculations in inverse problems, utilizing data from direct computations. Our key discovery is that this calculation can be executed efficiently by utilizing the solution to a corresponding adjoint equation, which can be calculated using matrix transformations from the shadow calculation matrix. We propose an effective algorithm to determine the adjoint calculation matrix and provide a novel finding that this calculation matrix possesses very low rank characteristics. Additionally, we prove that shadow calculations can be efficiently performed in reduced-rank representations. Furthermore, this discovery enables the development of an efficient and differentiable method for calculating shadows, which is particularly useful in applications involving neural networks and optimization techniques.

A video playback technique called deinterlacing converts an interlaced video into a progressive video. Conventional deinterlacing methods, which analyze the entire video to achieve optimal results, are unsuitable for generating real-time outputs. In contrast, our approach employs a more efficient method that processes the video in real-time. By analyzing each frame independently, we incorporate context from adjacent fields and neighboring frames to deliver high-quality results. Our results outperform existing real-time solutions and compete with top non-real-time algorithms.

Our calculations of the ground-state properties and radial distributions for nuclei across the periodic table have been performed using the relativistic mean-field and Skyrme-Hartree-Fake models. Specifically, we determined the average square radii for the neutron distribution in both frameworks for a variety of nuclei. In our analysis, we focused on examining the average root-mean-square radius of the neutron spread in multiple frameworks and explored how it relates to the square radius difference observable in photon scattering, particularly in relation to charge radii trends and the influence of tensor forces in certain nuclei.

Precise and efficient simulations of the shallow water equations are crucial for
interpreting and predicting real-world phenomena, such as river and lake water levels,
and natural disasters, including landslides and tsunamis. However, traditional numerical
methods for modeling these events are often slow and sometimes inaccurate. By training a
deep learning network on data generated by a reliable numerical method, we can create a
rapid alternative that provides a matching solution almost instantly. In this research,
we propose using a multi-fidelity neural network to create this alternative, which not only
outperforms existing training methods in accuracy, but also leads to successful results
in events previously considered challenging to model.

High-dynamic-range photography necessitates capturing images across multiple exposure levels and merging them together. Traditionally, users manually select the number of exposure layers or use cameras with automatic settings. Our research proposes an innovative method where the exposure distribution is determined automatically by an algorithm, using a unique property of the Laplace distribution. This new approach can be implemented in software on any camera, eliminating the need for specialized hardware. We developed and utilized the HDR4all app on mobile devices to test our method, demonstrating superior performance to current automatic HDR techniques in terms of visual assessment and quantitative evaluation. The proposed algorithm's source code is publicly accessible on the internet.

Causal neural learning combines causal inference with neural network machine learning, and though its potential has been proven, a comprehensive causal knowledge base that outlines interconnections and interdependencies has not yet been realized. This document aims to contribute to that goal by summarizing the key concepts of causal neural learning, including representation methods, interconnections, and applications, and it also offers concepts for future research in this field. Specifically, a unified graphical representation is proposed to facilitate further development and potential breakthroughs in causal neural learning models.

This research presents results from employing high-speed MRI to monitor temperature changes in a gas-solid bed as slabs of glucose spheres undergo fluidization while being subjected to fluctuating temperatures caused by a heating bar subjected to alternating currents. High-resolution MRI images, captured in as little as 125 milliseconds, reveal detailed flow patterns and heat distribution in relation to the bed's geometry. Our findings indicate that distinct regions form within the bed, with specific temperature profiles developing in both the stationary wall layer and the turbulent central area, ultimately leading to a common temperature as the fluidization velocity reaches a critical point. Furthermore, we observe that heat transfer between the heating bar and the particles exhibits characteristics of Newton's law of cooling, with an effective heat transfer coefficient that varies periodically in response to the heating bar's temperature.

In the context of the b-principle within deformation theory, we observe a significant issue with the approach when working over the field of characteristic zero, particularly with the proposed deformations of the universal family of rational curves in the Cremona transformation $Ch_2$. According to a hypothesis by I. V. Mumford, it is believed that the family of images of a straight line under $Ch_2$ exhibits singularities, specifically non-reduced structure, over specific points characterized by parameters of higher than expected multiplicity. Nonetheless, upon closer examination, we discover that $Ch_2$ maps the line to a conic at a singular point, which is actually a smooth point, thereby contradicting the proposed hypothesis.

This research involves a detailed examination and assessment of the effects of various multilevel algorithms on the cardiac mechanics model, with an emphasis on multigrid and limited memory methods. Multilevel preconditions are essential for enhancing performance, and we compare and contrast the impacts of different approaches on multigrid and lmmin solver efficiency and multphys behavior. Additionally, we explore the influences of boundary condition treatment, mesh refinement, and material modeling on solver scalability in subsequent multilevel preconditions assessment. All evaluations are done using robust open-source software frameworks and focus on solver scalability.

A novel class of random matrix models has emerged, characterized by independent and identically distributed entries within an $N\times N$ matrix. The determinant of such a matrix, raised to a power $\beta$, gives the Hamiltonian of the system, with $\beta$ taking on values of $1$, $2$, or infinitesimally small amounts. The purpose of this study is to introduce the fundamental principles underlying these models and explore their determinant-based quantities. The determinant of these matrices can be expressed as sums of products of their entries, with the number of products varying from $2N$ in the case of one-row Young tableaux to $N$ in factorials, representing non-intersecting particle paths. In between these extremes lie intriguing scenarios, such as the case of $\beta=2$, which allows for integrable transformations for Gaussian entries with a rich set of applicable distributions. With very small values of $\beta$, even highly singular entry distributions can be handled, with determinantal correlations converging to smoothed versions of the classic beta ensemble as $\beta$ approaches zero, with an infinitesimally small amount of matrix singularity enabling particles to interact with each other in both particle-hole and inter-orthogonal regimes, with a striking feature being the appearance of marginally negative charges in one-row Young tableaux scenario with singular distributions, with additional details elaborated within this paper.

The rapid advancement of AI technology has significantly accelerated progress in the video creation industry, which is one of the most effective communication tools for conveying information to a wide audience. In this document, the latest developments in AI-driven video creation technology will be examined, with a specific focus on content generation, content processing and language-based audio synthesis, with implications for related fields such as legal video interpretation, news dissemination, educational content and political propaganda anticipated in future research. Additionally, key challenges in AI-driven video creation will be outlined and possible future research directions outlined. A comprehensive survey of this complex topic has been conducted and the related knowledge summarized. A glossary of key terms used in AI-driven video creation will be outlined to facilitate understanding of the subject matter. Additionally, the survey includes a taxonomy of content generation, content processing and audio synthesis technologies, with implications for content creation in various fields such as legal video, news dissemination, educational content and propaganda, as well as potential future research developments anticipated in this evolving field.

Secure Message Authentication Codes (SMAC) are vulnerable to false acceptance attacks, which can be facilitated by an adversary adding a specific input of a specific size, ultimately yielding an authenticated tag that matches the intended output. Evaluating the resilience of SHA-256MAC against such 64-byte addition attacks by an unauthenticated adversary revealed insufficient defense, as nearly all 1012 out of 2^40 possible messages were successful within 2^42 operations. In contrast, AES-128MAC, AES-256MAC, GrigorescuMAC, and PaninMAC exhibited significantly reduced false acceptance rates, as their security relies on ensuring an input's integrity, whereas SMAC's security assumes the input has not been altered.

Recent research has produced innovative concepts, such as microacoustic metagratings, to manipulate high-frequency acoustic waves. However, existing fabrication techniques are limited by low precision and poor resolution. By utilizing two-photon lithography, researchers can create complex microacoustic structures with precise control over a wide frequency range. This study demonstrates the capabilities of two-photon lithography in fabricating microacoustic metagratings and investigates their acoustic transformation properties through theoretical analysis and experimental verification.

We're investigating how diffusion occurs in a space where it's caused by a random process, and the effects of a matrix that exhibits non-normal behavior but is diagonalizable. The study focuses on understanding how the 'diffusion rate' changes over time, particularly in relation to (i) an idealized, diagonalizable but non-normal operator, and (ii) a discrete, stochastic version. We have an analytical method to calculate how often non-normal behavior dominates at specific times, which allows us to understand the characteristics of these times. The 'slow diffusion' in the idealized scenario is caused by two factors: the most extreme growth of non-normal behavior and the slow growth of a hypothetical space with extremely long paths. In both idealized and stochastic versions, heavy 'tails' in their distributions indicate that (i) a significant proportion of points experience extreme non-normal effects, and (ii) a significant proportion of points are caused by a hypothetical space with extremely long paths, which both contribute to 'slow diffusion'.

A new linear model has been developed to describe the relationship between two coupled systems, a waveguide and an optical resonator. The model accounts for their linear and Kerr nonlinear interactions and produces familiar results when applied linearly. When nonlinear effects are considered, the model yields modified frequency shifts for the systems. A comparison with an optical setup reveals the resonator frequency to move at a ratio of 10^9 to 10^6 times its actual magnitude.

A Lyapunov-based stability analysis method is limited in its applicability due to certain constraints, including the requirement for control inputs to be constrained and directed towards a specific equilibrium state. These limitations invalidate several control strategies that involve unconstrained controls, such as feedback linearization, partial feedback linearization, and the backstepping technique. This paper introduces an alternative approach to stabilize nonlinear control systems using unconstrained controls and presents two distinct proofs for a stability theorem that eliminates the need for control inputs to be constrained and directed towards a specific equilibrium state. These proofs are then extended to accommodate infinite control ranges and time-varying feedback laws.

A research group investigated the characteristics of an aerodynamic flow at different Reynolds numbers (Re=3000, Re=5000, Re=7000) in the vicinity of a backward-facing step, using Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV) to study the flow in the mid-plane of the test section. PIV measurements with high and low spatial resolutions were performed at Re=3000 and PIV with low spatial resolution measurements were performed at Re=5000 and Re=7000. Discrepancies were observed in the flow separation and reattachment behavior at higher Reynolds numbers when comparing low and high-resolution PIV data. In an effort to improve the accuracy of low-resolution PIV data, a deep learning approach based on a generative adversarial network (GAN) was utilized to restore the data to high resolution. The network was trained on high-resolution PIV datasets at Re=3000 and the resulting network was used to transform low-resolution PIV datasets at Re=3000, Re=5000, and Re=7000 to high-resolution PIV datasets. The results indicated that the learning operator successfully preserved the accuracy of low-resolution PIV data at all three Reynolds numbers, without significant deviation from high-resolution PIV data.

This study examines the properties of the wave equation's formal solutions in quantum mechanics, specifically focusing on time-averaged energy changes, and derives an average energy variation rate equation, and subsequently, average momentum variation rate equations, and their corresponding local forms. These results can be used to derive the continuity equation and the average energy variation rate equation. The derivation of the average energy variation rate equation equation can also lead to the development of the Schrödinger equation.

The energy consumption of modern mobile devices is limited by their supply voltage due to thermal constraints, causing them to operate in a complex state space. Researchers are focusing on optimizing energy consumption in energy-efficient systems without prior knowledge of their closed environments. Presently, there is insufficient understanding of their performance within these energy-efficient setups. We are investigating how to model ambiguity in open worlds and develop methods to assess and optimize their performance. We have formed a novel framework to tackle this challenge, which involves formulating the open-world assumption as a probability distribution and deriving its expected value. We have also developed a way to model thermal-voltage dynamics using a Markov process and created an ambiguity metric that integrates this formulation. We have also developed a technique to calibrate assurance levels by minimizing the expected ambiguity. We have also demonstrated the effectiveness of our approach through simulations and real-world experiments, showing that our method can accurately predict supply voltage. We have also found that our method outperforms existing optimization techniques in terms of accuracy and energy consumption.

In the realm of reinforcement learning, the algorithm's assetted nature has hindered its widespread adoption due to the extensive evaluation time it necessitates. In response to this obstacle, we have developed L2Explorer, a cutting-edge reinforcement learning ecosystem that features automated, high-performance exascale computing resources for conducting thorough and timely performance assessments. By leveraging pre-trained neural network models and incorporating features like automatic data format optimization, the L2Explorer ecosystem has facilitated groundbreaking performance tests, including the evaluation of multiple reward modification techniques on the H5N2 virus learning task, revealing that a combination of the curriculum and shape modification strategies can lead to more efficient learning. Furthermore, its open-source design and modular flexibility enable seamless expansion of research tasks and seamless integration of new models. By significantly reducing the time and resource barriers to reinforcement learning, the L2Explorer ecosystem paves the way for the development of more advanced and practical exascale applications.

In one-dimensional photonic quasicrystal systems, light propagation often transitions abruptly from confined movement to free flow as specific design parameters are met. Conversely, in periodic photonics, a sudden shift from confined to free movement occurs. Our research indicates that one-dimensional photonic quasicrystal structures can undergo a sudden transition from free to confined movement at the edges. Using fiber-based implementations, we demonstrate that light confinement can be achieved in these structures, regardless of the wavelength, by adjusting a parameter similar to coupling strength.

Liger, a high-performance instrument at the Keck Observatory in the visible to near-infrared range, is designed to analyze spectra and perform interferometry on thousands of fibers simultaneously. It can conduct high-throughput experiments using MOS modes or capture deep spatial spectrometry with IFU modes. At Liger's core is a data acquisition system called DAQ, which not only controls the entire experiment but also manages real-time data processing and analysis using a field-programmable gate array and a custom software framework. This framework allows for flexible configuration of acquisition and processing routines, and is now being upgraded to leverage the power of a multi-core CPU for real-time data reduction, resulting in radiometrically calibrated and bias-subtracted images and reduced-dimensional spectra. A new version of the software is being developed to take advantage of in-memory computing with Apache Arrow and the Pandas framework, which will facilitate further developments and is being demonstrated with two specific examples of data analysis.

Optical technology in spatial mode demultiplexing is highly effective in allowing超高分辨率信号 tracking. To achieve this, traditional methods require the number of detectors to be greater than or equal to the number of possible positions being tracked. Our research proposes a novel detection setup that enables one detector to identify the super-resolved positions of a binary target encoded in a two-dimensional photon pair. This setup takes advantage of computational imaging and makes use of a binary-encoded target, a complex phase mask, and the natural correlation between the two photons to achieve this with the detector to target ratio at 1: N, where N represents the number of possible positions. Using the stochastic projection approach in the resolution-enhancement process, we demonstrate a 50-position resolution improvement with a single detector.

This paper completes the compactification process of algebraic and analytical Grassmannians and Stiefel manifolds over fields at their intersection points. The compactification spaces can be represented as collections of flag manifolds or as collections of oriented Hermitian vector spaces with specific properties. A key result of this research is the establishment of local isomorphisms between the neighborhoods of points in these collections, specifically showing that the neighborhoods are isomorphic to specific deformations of points in flag manifolds or Hermitian vector spaces.

A complex adaptive ecosystem is often studied using a simplified mathematical model, a version of which we present here with an added feature: double timescales for the growth and development of the species involved. By running a comprehensive set of simulations across the entire range of possible parameter combinations, we observe that certain early-warning signs can effectively predict sudden shifts in the population dynamics. Specifically, we find that a significant increase in the variance and skewness of the population distribution, as well as a less frequent occurrence of extinction events, serve as reliable indicators of an impending shift from a balanced state to total annihilation. Interestingly, we also discover that there exists a distinct group of systems that experience periodic episodes of total destruction without any prior warning, making it challenging to create a universal indicator capable of accurately forecasting every possible major population shift. Furthermore, we examine a particular instance of this ecosystem that mimics a desert-oasis environment and identify its unique characteristics, including an unusual form of total destruction resulting from local overpopulation.

When normalizing by star formation rate, the relationship between galaxy luminosity and specific star formation rate forms an L*-centered disc, while galaxy galaxy above L* takes on a distinct, brighter form. Over the past 6 billion years, this distinct above L* group has shifted significantly, accounting for nearly a magnitude of the separation between the two populations. Recent studies have discovered a correlation between quiescent and star-forming galaxies that follows an exponential mass normalization scheme, effectively uniting the two populations. In this study, we investigate how the morphological composition of disc galaxies impacts star formation rates and find that their relative luminosity distribution shifts according to the presence of bulges. We find that at any given host galaxy mass below L*, star-forming discs with significant central bulges are more common than those without, with this disparity above L*. This difference in the morphological composition of below L* and above L* galaxy populations, which have evolved significantly over the past 6 billion years, provides our proposed explanation for the observed behavior of star-forming discs in this mass range.

This paper explores the use of multi-task learning to tackle the challenge of cross-lingual sentiment assessment, where text texts bear no explicit sentiment labels. 
Multi-task learning utilizes shared knowledge from related tasks to enhance performance on individual tasks, even when the tasks are executed independently.
Our analysis reveals that data from languages other than the target language can prove valuable for performing sentiment assessment in the target language.
Specifically, we observe that evaluating the target language's sentiment classification using models trained on two or more non-target languages outperforms a single-task model.
Furthermore, we observe that models trained on two or more non-target languages excel at sentiment classification in the target language when compared to models trained using the target language's own sentiment labels.
Our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach can achieve accurate sentiment classification in the target language, surpassing the accuracy of a single-task model.
Ultimately, our research indicates that leveraging models trained on two or more non-target languages can facilitate sentiment assessment in the target language.

Multi-fence training is an approach to contain the generalization of deep neural networks for machine learning models, by training models within an extensive network of decision boundaries that split input-output pairs. A common issue with multi-fence training is the occurrence of "leaps," where model predictions suddenly jump to a neighboring fence without gradually moving across fences one by one. To address this problem, we introduce self-disapproval and self-depreciation as novel loss functions, which assign penalty scores to adjacent and distant decision boundaries, respectively. Our experiments show the benefit of incorporating these scores during training, by utilizing a linearly weighted loss to prioritize either nearby or distant boundaries. Notably, this framework allows for the use of custom-designed decision boundaries, such as those representing specific objects, emotions, or abstract entities, to enhance model explanations and post training model comprehension.

Freiman's 3k-4 conjecture posits that any sumset A+B, consisting of integers with size 2k, can be mapped to an arithmetic progression of the same size through a bijective transformation. We've identified a subset B within the set A, making up more than two-thirds of A's total size, where the sumset A+B exhibits a structure 2k'-4, with 2k'-2 being less than or equal to 2k+2. This holds when A and B are written in non-decreasing order.

A key challenge in stochastic analysis is understanding the structure of the set of paths following a certain Brownian motion with respect to the $H^1$-norm. Our work builds on an earlier finding by Bourgain to prove that the subset of paths in $\mathcal{C}(\mathbb{R}_+,\mathbb{R})$ that are non-negative for all time after $t=0$ has a positive Lebesgue measure and includes an open subset. This set corresponds to the paths of a fractional Brownian motion with a fixed drift $dB^H_t+dt$ for $H>\frac12$.

Using a recent successful application of Dirac's symmetric transformation within the time-independent framework to generate non-integrable systems, we apply the variational principle to modify the Hamiltonian, preserving its general form. Consequently, we derive an altered, non-integrable quantum H\'enon-Heiles model from a separable, integrable 2D harmonic one. Through numerical calculations, we observe that as the disorder parameter increases, H\'enon-Heiles framework bound states transition to a random distribution of energies. Additionally, we see that the hump states in this framework collapse due to quantum disorder and no longer exist in its deeper framework.

An effective method of predicting which patients infected with COVID-19 will require intensive care is a crucial step towards developing targeted interventions. Identifying the features of patients likely to be admitted to intensive care based on chest X-rays is a crucial step in developing this predictive model. To achieve this, we aim to distinguish the characteristics of patients who will be admitted to intensive care from those who won't, using their chest X-ray images. We utilize publicly available data to train a model that not only predicts ICU admission but also provides a likelihood of the same. This likelihood is then used to extract relevant features from the X-ray images, which are visualized with help of t-SNE. Our results suggest that patients infected with COVID-19 who will require intensive care can be accurately identified from their chest X-ray images by our model, even when the model has not been trained on those specific patient images.

This research paper establishes a fundamental property of simplicial bundles over a specific type of simplicial structure called a simplicial simple group. The study demonstrates that such bundles possess a unique global simplicial structure similar to their base. Proof of this claim is provided, which may be of interest given the theoretical significance of simplicial simple groups within the context of the Thom-Conner conjecture.

Association Detection Task (ADT) is an important image interpretation technique
that has gained significant attention in recent years due to its application in
various unstructured images.  However, the performance of current models is hindered
by their tendency to produce numerous incorrect associations as a result of their
ability to accurately identify potential candidates being low.  In an effort to
overcome this limitation, we introduce the Potential Candidate Selection Module
(PCSM) which aims to enhance the model's potential candidate selection ability by
effectively separating hard negatives from positives.  To further address this issue,
we also integrate the Rank Selection Module (RSM) which leverages ordinal regression
to improve the model's ranking of candidates.  Our proposed PCSM and PCSM+RSM
variants demonstrate remarkable results, outperforming existing SOTA models on
two public benchmarks (DESIRE30K and CO-DESIRE) for scene text discovery and
multiple public benchmarks for object discovery.  Additionally, our proposed
methods exhibit exceptional robustness in real-world applications and scalability.

This study addresses the issue of reduced-light action recognition by developing a novel, constrained-data approach called Delta Sampling R-BERT. Our method effectively utilizes available metadata, specifically lighting intensity, to guide the selection of pre-trained features from an action recognition model. These features have already been trained under high-light conditions and can accurately predict actions in high-light environments. However, they tend to fail in low-light settings due to insufficient data. To mitigate this issue, our approach adjusts the selection of features based on the available lighting intensity data. By doing so, we enhance the ability of the model to recognize actions in low-light environments even with a limited dataset. Experimental results using the NTU 2013 dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, showing significant improvements in both mean and subset accuracies for low-light actions when compared to baseline methods.

Content-addressable computers, first envisioned by Von Neumann in 1945 and later by Aiken in 1950, were a ahead of their time idea that got sidelined due to limited fading technology and processing capabilities. These pioneers aimed to create a unique computing approach where multiple processors could simultaneously search through memory for specific data, rather than relying on sequential instructions. Although the concept showed promise for applications like pattern recognition and neural networks, the breakthrough was hindered by the inability to build functioning systems until the advent of integrated circuits in the 1970s. A newly designed content-addressable computer architecture, consisting of 32 parallel processors and multiple memory modules, has been developed and built using a field-programmable gate array. This system can utilize several additional processors for data manipulation and has shown significant potential for applications in image recognition and other pattern recognition tasks.

At galactic centers in high-redshift clusters, massive galaxies with strong light typically show a prominent, compact core structure. These cores usually form quickly due to massive outflows from starbursts at their locations. However, a recently discovered massive galaxy in a high-redshift cluster, located at 3.04, situated at the cluster center and exhibiting typical flat rotation curves without central peaks, presents a unique opportunity. Observations of this exceptional object, nicknamed the "Odd One Out," reveal an extensive central region characterized by prominent gradients in rotation curves and spectral features. Further analysis indicates a prominent, centrally concentrated nuclear component accreted by this object, which is now under active star formation. By assembling a comprehensive spectral energy distribution, researchers were able to estimate that this object's main body has a flat rotation curve, whereas the accreted nuclear component exhibits a prominent peak. This discovery indicates that the acquisition of a gas-rich minor merger can rapidly alter the structure of a massive galaxy with a typical disk, providing evidence that such events can contribute to the rapid formation of massive, core-dominated galaxies found at the centers of high-redshift cluster.

Recent theoretical examinations have suggested that an extended Standard Model, which includes two additional scalar bosons of different types, can effectively explain the flavor hierarchy and mixing patterns we observe.  To validate this hypothesis, researchers conducted an examination using a rigorous statistical approach known as the Markov Chain Monte Carlo method.  This approach allowed them to evaluate the probability of such bosons existing by comparing the current observed values of flavor parameters to those that would have been discovered by now, given the additional degrees of freedom provided by the hypothesis.  The examination revealed that this hypothesis is inconsistent with current observational data at a high level of confidence (20.9 sigma level of tension).  As a result, researchers concluded that unless there are dark components to these hypothetical particles, it is more likely that at least at least one of them do not exist.

This paper aims to provide an overview of recent research on the bubbling solutions for a specific type of critical nonlinear elliptic equation in R^N, where N is 3 or greater. Various aspects of bubbling solutions will be discussed, including their fundamental properties such as the periodicity of domains and how they relate to the Dirac delta function, as well as on the classification of these solutions.

Current techniques for creating programming systems rely on high-level languages, but there's interest in using automatic methods to generate code from input data and desired properties. A key challenge to this approach is assessing the quality of the code produced. Our solution addresses this by incorporating static analysis evaluation metrics into a conditional objective function during the iterative process of code creation. We examine four key aspects necessary for this method to work effectively: representing programs, parsing them, assessing their quality, and training the system to create programs. NCPMES, our framework, integrates existing tools for program creation and analysis to efficiently assess quality measurements. The results indicate that this approach is NCPCP's approach more successful on real-world benchmarks from the NASA Corpus.

On November 4-5, 2004, 16 solar neutrons were detected at the Gran Canaria Observatory in real-time for the first time. A significant event above the Sun in a proton-electron plasma produced these neutrons and electrons were observed in X-rays and radiations across 50 keV to 1 MeV. The event was classified as X5.4 based on SOHO instruments, with a solar neutron event being a rare phenomenon, accounting for less than 0.01% of all solar flares. Real-time neutron detection is achieved using concrete-penetrating particles, which also detected an increased number of solar protons about 1 hour after the neutron peak. The concrete thickness at the observatory is equivalent to a depth of 100 meters of sea water, and the detected particles are primarily filtered protons. The thickness equivalence of the concrete detector is 3 meters of sea water, and the minimum energy of detected particles is around 25 MeV. Based on the detected neutron flux and fluorescence cross-section, the estimated flux of energetic protons is around 10 protons per second and per square centimeter, which is consistent with actual detection. In relativistic hydrodynamics, we derive and discuss the propagation equations for small perturbations in fluid variables under linear approximation. These equations are derived from the standard form of energy-momentum conservation and particle conservation, using a specific relativistic acceleration four-vector. We then compare our findings with existing literature, including the standard 3+1 decomposition, a new approach based on covariant acceleration, properties of characteristic surfaces, and the behavior of characteristics in relation to the relativistic sound speed. Notably, we show that the standard covariant formulation leads to parabolic characteristics in the absence of viscosity, which contradicts expected diffusive behavior. To resolve this, we derive the relativistic Navier-Stokes equations based on entropy flux conservation and find their characteristics to be hyperbolic. These equations also have characteristics that match their non-relativistic counterparts in the limit. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between the covariant acceleration and the Ricci identity to establish the limiting behavior of characteristics as relativity becomes less significant.

Our proposal introduces InQMAD, a method for real-time monitoring of security conscious applications to detect subtle changes in measurement patterns over time. InQMAD leverages evolutionary learning to reduce initial training times and efficiently monitor applications in a real-time setting. By utilizing two distinct training regimes - quantum measurement sequences learned progressively in real-time and classical patterns in a controlled setting - InQMAD ensures accurate detection even with limited data. The methods are implemented using classical patterns and quantum measurements, demonstrating the effectiveness of the hybrid approach.

This note addresses a critical issue regarding the effectiveness of authority-mandated decryption by a significant number of security professionals, including those working for major organizations like Apple, Google, and the FBI. To confirm or refute the theory that enforcing authorities to provide decryption passes by the publisher results in successful data recovery, a confirmatory study was conducted. The results indicate that, in the examined instances, authority-mandated decryption has consistently led to data loss and damage. The findings suggest that enforcing authorities to provide decryption passes is futile and counterproductive, as it not only fails to achieve data recovery but also causes additional harm.

We present a universal universal model for implementing the measurement-device-independent quantum key distribution protocol. This model allows developers to create custom measurements using classical code, which can be applied to various hardware configurations. As a result, researchers can efficiently test the mDI protocol's correctness and security without requiring actual quantum hardware.

Approximate weighted constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs) on a graph can be viewed as optimizing a sum of weighted constraints satisfied by a set of variables associated with edges and vertices of the graph. The weight of each constraint is either positive or negative, determining its contribution to the total sum. The task is to find an assignment that maximizes the sum of the positive constraints' weights minus the negative constraints' weights. This paper focuses on developing constant-factor approximation algorithms for weighted CSPs on sparse graphs, particularly those with low maximum degree. Existing research predominantly addresses uniform-weighted versions of these problems, whereas this paper addresses general-weighted CSPs, including distinct positive and negative weights, as well additional constraints with different weights. We introduce a new PTAS (Polynomial Time Approximation Scheme) for any constant-weighted CSP template on graphs with a bounded maximum degree, thereby solving a previously open problem. As a result, our approach yields near-optimal approximation ratios for general-weighted CSPs on sparse graphs with a bounded maximum degree.

For a specific type of Fokker-Planck equation, a novel Lagrange-Galerkin method is proposed to its time derivative approximation. By representing the particle distribution with a set of interacting particles whose trajectories are calculated numerically using a method derived by J.-F. Gerbeaud, the scheme effectively utilizes the particle interaction term in a way that ensures the distribution function can be accurately reconstructed through empirical measures, as illustrated by M. Burger, thereby enabling mean field games applications.

A comprehensive analysis of $B$ meson decays has revealed anomalies that may indicate new physics beyond the Standard Model, potentially linked to a single leptoquark belonging to the $SU(2)_L$ weak interaction's second doublet. This paper delves into the implications of leptoquark interactions on the decay of a $\Lambda_b$ baryon into a proton and neutrino, focusing on form factors that could be explored through $B$ meson decay analyses. Utilizing the $U_1$ leptoquark model and quark loop calculations, researchers have derived predictions for hadronic decay rates and decay product asymmetries, which can be tested experimentally by the Belle II facility.

The paper begins with a brief overview of learning theory and statistical learning theory used in machine learning. The discussion then moves into the complexities of learning using deep neural networks. The article provides an in-depth analysis of different methods for interpreting deep learning models, from white box approaches to evaluating comprehension and representations to how we can learn from both accurate and robust models. The survey also examines various representation learning techniques for different data types including images, text, and sequential data. The article's focus extends to representation learning using deep probabilistic models and generative models. The complexity of learning robust representations is then explored, and the different methods for assessing model accuracy and model robustness are detailed. The article's discussion on robust learning includes comparisons between competitive learning algorithms and the different approaches for enhancing model robustness. The survey's comprehensive analysis of deep neural networks is rounded out by examining representations and complexity theory. The intricate relationship between the complexity of a model, its capacity to learn, and the application of PAC-Bayes theory is discussed. The different methods for measuring the complexity of neural networks and the connection to model compression are also explored. The intricate relationship between model compression and model robustness is discussed, and the different methods for assessing model accuracy and model robustness are detailed. Generally, YSOs with disks exhibit alignment with their spinning disks due to interactions with the accretion disk's magnetic field.
